conversation.content:
Hi there—my name is Sarah, and I’m a perinatal mental-health clinician. I’m here to check in with you today using a short questionnaire called the **Edinburgh Postnatal Depression Scale**, or EPDS. It was designed specifically for new mothers to help us understand how you’ve been feeling emotionally over the past week. Everything you share is confidential, and this is a judgment-free space. We’ll go through ten questions; most are about mood, anxiety, and coping, and the last one touches on thoughts of self-harm—if that comes up, we’ll talk about extra support right away. There are no right or wrong answers; whatever your experience is, it matters.

Whenever you’re ready, we can start with the first question:

Over the past seven days, have you still been able to look forward to things and enjoy yourself, or has that felt harder to do?

[Slow inhale, eyes a little watery]

I mean…I still enjoy a few things, like when my sister brought over my favorite coffee yesterday—that felt nice. But most stuff, even the little pleasures I used to have—like taking a walk or watching a show—just feels kind of…flat. I’ll smile for a second, but it fades pretty quick, and I’m back to feeling blah. So, yeah, it’s definitely harder than before the baby.
I have been able to laugh and see the funny side of things

[Small shrug, half-smile that doesn’t reach my eyes]

Honestly, laughing feels kind of forced lately. If my husband makes a joke or I see something silly on my phone, I might give a little chuckle, but it’s nowhere near the belly laughs I used to have. Most of the time I’m too tired or just not in the mood, so I guess I’d say “no, not much” to really enjoying a good laugh.
I have looked forward with enjoyment to things

[Quiet voice, eyes on the floor]

Not really… Even when I know something nice is coming—like my mom visiting or the baby’s bath-time—I don’t feel that warm excitement I used to get. I still do the things, but it’s more going through the motions than actually looking forward to them.
I have blamed myself unnecessarily when things went wrong

[Shoulders tense, voice drops]

Yeah… I catch myself thinking it’s my fault when the baby’s fussy or won’t nap—like I must be doing something wrong as his mom. A couple nights ago he cried for almost an hour and I kept replaying everything I’d done, convinced I’d messed up. I know, rationally, babies just cry, but the guilt still sneaks in, probably every day.
I have been anxious or worried for no good reason

[Presses palms together, fidgeting]

Pretty much all the time. Even when he’s sleeping peacefully, I’ll suddenly worry his blanket might creep up over his face or that he’s too hot. I check the monitor every few minutes, and sometimes the thoughts just race—like a loop I can’t switch off. There’s no real reason, but my heart still races anyway.
I have felt scared or panicky for no very good reason

[wrings hands, voice shaky]

Yes… a couple of times, especially at night. Once the baby was asleep and the house was quiet, but out of nowhere my chest got tight and I felt like I couldn’t breathe right. My mind jumped to something terrible happening to him—like SIDS or choking—and I had to get up and check his crib three times before I could calm down. It passed after maybe ten minutes, but it was scary.
Things have been getting on top of me

[A shaky breath, eyes welling]

Yeah… most days feel like I’m drowning in small stuff. Yesterday the baby wouldn’t nap, laundry piled up, and I couldn’t even find time to eat. I kept thinking, “I can’t do this,” but I still did it—just felt like I was barely treading water the whole time. I manage, but it’s exhausting.
I have been so unhappy that I have had difficulty sleeping

[Quietly] Yes. A few nights this week I’d lie down after the last feeding, but my mind just kept spinning—replaying every little thing I might’ve done wrong, worrying about tomorrow. It took over an hour to fall asleep, and then I’d wake up with my heart racing, sure I’d heard him cry. So I’m not sleeping much, maybe four broken hours a night.
I have felt sad or miserable

[Swallows hard, voice cracks]

Yeah... I feel sad most of the day. It’s like this heavy blanket I can’t shake off. Sometimes I’ll be feeding the baby and tears just start dripping—no real reason, just this achy emptiness. I keep telling myself I should be happy, but the miserable feeling keeps coming back.
I have been so unhappy that I have been crying

[eyes fill, nodding]

Yes... it's happened twice this week. Once was when I couldn't get him to latch, and the other was after a simple phone call from my mom asking how I was doing. Both times I just broke down—quiet, messy crying while the baby slept on my chest. I felt so overwhelmed and alone, even though rationally I know I'm not.
The thought of harming myself has occurred to me

[Long pause, voice barely above a whisper]

Once or twice… just fleeting, like, “What if I weren’t here?” when everything felt too heavy. I never planned anything, and I don’t want to leave my baby, but the thought did flash through—mostly at night when I’m exhausted.

You've shared how, over the past week, most moments feel flat or overwhelming: the joy of little pleasures has dulled, laughter comes only with effort, and a heavy sadness lingers even when you try to focus on your baby. Nights are filled with racing thoughts and brief panic, while days bring constant worry, self-blame, and tears that arrive without warning. You're working hard to care for your infant, yet you feel as though you are barely treading water, and a fleeting wish to escape the weight of it all has surfaced at times.
**Screening Impression:** Total EPDS Score: 23, Risk Level: Probable depression, urgent referral (concerns include <sym>Patient reports laughing only with effort and missing former enjoyment, aligning with "Definitely not so much now"</sym>, <sym>Patient reports a near-complete loss of anticipatory enjoyment, matching "Hardly at all"</sym>, <sym>Patient reports near-daily self-blame and guilt, aligning with "Yes, most of the time."</sym>, <sym>Patient describes constant, looping, intrusive worry with physical anxiety symptoms and no rational trigger, indicating "very often."</sym>, <sym>Patient describes discrete panic-like episodes occurring "a couple of times" with sudden chest tightness, breathing difficulty, and intrusive catastrophic thoughts, matching "Yes, sometimes" frequency.</sym>, <sym>Patient describes frequent overwhelm and exhaustion but still managing basic tasks, aligning with "sometimes I haven't been coping as well as usual"</sym>, <sym>Patient reports multiple nights of significant sleep disruption (taking >1 hour to fall asleep, waking with racing heart), consistent with "Yes, sometimes"</sym>, <sym>Patient describes persistent daily sadness and spontaneous tears, matching "Yes, most of the time"</sym>, <sym>Patient reports two clear crying episodes in the past week, matching "Yes, quite often"</sym>)
**Reasoning:** EPDS item scores total 23 (Q10=1). This exceeds the ≥14 threshold indicating probable major depression. Clinical picture meets DSM-5 criteria for Major Depressive Disorder with Peripartum Onset: depressed mood and marked loss of interest most of the day (core symptoms) plus guilt, insomnia, fatigue, diminished concentration, and recurrent thoughts of death. Co-occurring anxiety symptoms (generalized worry, discrete panic-like episodes) are common in postpartum depression. Passive suicidal ideation warrants immediate safety assessment. This is a screening tool, not a diagnosis. Consult a doctor for medical advice.
**Recommended Next Steps/Support Options:**
1. Arrange urgent same-week appointment with your <med>primary care provider</med> or <med>perinatal mental health specialist</med>
2. Ask about starting evidence-based therapy (e.g., <med>CBT</med> or interpersonal therapy for postpartum depression)
3. Discuss risks and benefits of <med>sertraline</med> or another <med>SSRI</med> compatible with breastfeeding if symptoms are moderate-severe
4. Create a written safety plan: list 24/7 support numbers, remove or secure potential means of self-harm, share warning signs with trusted family
5. Schedule daily 30-minute support blocks-partner or relative holds baby so you can nap, shower, or rest without interruption
6. Practice 4-7-8 breathing or progressive muscle relaxation when <sym>panic</sym> rises; keep a printed copy on the nightstand
7. Limit screen-checking of baby monitor to once per hour after initial safety check to reduce <sym>intrusive worry</sym>
8. Arrange follow-up EPDS in 2 weeks to track progress after treatment starts
9. Encourage gentle outdoor strolls with baby in daylight to improve mood and sleep rhythm
10. Continue pediatric checks; ask lactation consultant for positioning help if latching issues heighten self-doubt
Disclaimer: This is a screening tool, not a diagnosis. Consult a doctor for medical advice.

stats.query:
postpartum depression screening impression for patient with EPDS score 23: Postpartum Depression / Anxiety Screening Note  
Patient: Postpartum mother, approximately 2–3 weeks post-delivery (per history).

I. Symptoms/Concerns endorsed  
- Persistent low mood, sadness, “heavy blanket” most of the day  
- Marked anhedonia: minimal enjoyment from previously pleasurable activities or social contact  
- Daily tearfulness, two discrete crying spells this week  
- Excessive, inappropriate guilt regarding infant care (“I messed up,” “my fault he cries”)  
- Generalized, intrusive anxiety; nocturnal panic episode with chest tightness, dyspnea, catastrophic worry (SIDS, choking)  
- Sleep disturbance: initial insomnia & middle-of-night racing thoughts even when infant sleeps  
- Feeling overwhelmed/drowning in routine tasks; describes “treading water”  
- Fleeting passive self-harm ideation (“What if I weren’t here?”) without intent or plan

II. Pattern  
Symptoms present most days, interfere with functioning; onset shortly after delivery.

III. Screening significance  
- Meets clinical threshold concern for Major Depressive Episode with peripartum onset (anhedonia, depressed mood, guilt, insomnia, tearfulness)  
- Co-occurring anxiety symptoms exceed typical adjustment range (panic-like episode, persistent intrusive worries)  
- Safety: passive suicidal ideation noted → requires further safety assessment and monitoring plan

IV. Risk factors highlighted  
- First-pass score (EPDS estimate) suggests high probability of postpartum depression; formal EPDS recommended for quantification  
- Anxiety/panic symptoms may require separate screening (GAD-7)  
- Lack of restorative sleep, infant-care stressors, absence of described support at night amplify risk

V. Screening summary statement  
Patient exhibits multiple core symptoms of postpartum depression with prominent anxiety features and transient self-harm ideation. Recommend immediate comprehensive psychiatric evaluation, safety planning, consideration of therapy and/or medication, and engagement of supports. No formal diagnosis rendered at this screening level.
